body.text: Recommendation feeds and sharing features can expose harmful content to people beyond the original audience. As more users view, comment on, or share the content, online abuse can spread quickly and reach larger audiences.

Harmful comments on videos can remain visible long after they are posted, allowing abuse to continue over time. During livestreams, abusive messages can appear and multiply rapidly as viewers react in real time.

Replies, reposts, and mentions can spread abusive messages across public conversations. When many users join in, a single harmful comment can develop into repeated or coordinated attacks against an individual.

Harmful comments can spread within online communities as members respond, share, or encourage similar behaviour. Group discussions may reinforce negative attitudes and lead to repeated abuse targeting the same person.

Abusive messages can be forwarded or shared between individuals and groups, spreading harmful content through private conversations. Limited visibility outside these spaces can make it difficult to identify and address ongoing abuse.

html.text:
Matteo is a high-performing college volleyball athlete with ambitions of joining the national team.

Between demanding coursework and intensive training, he has been under considerable pressure and struggling to stay focused.

During an important match, Matteo serves into the net on match point, costing his team the match. The crowd reacts strongly, and some spectators begin shouting harsh criticism about his performance from the stands. The reaction continues as Matteo leaves the court.

Is this online abuse? No.

The criticism may be aggressive and harmful, but this is still happening offline. However, reactions that begin at a sporting event / on the ground, can quickly move into digital spaces, where they may reach a much wider audience.

After the match, the criticism moves online. A fan posts a video of Matteo’s missing serve, tags Matteo’s social media account, and adds insulting and humiliating comments intended to ridicule him.

The situation has become online abuse.

The fan is using insulting and humiliating content directed at Matteo through a digital platform. This is offensive speech.

By the next day, many users had joined in. Hostile comments are appearing across Matteo’s social media accounts, and the video of his missed serve is being repeatedly shared alongside insulting posts.

The situation has escalated to digital hostility.

What began with one user has developed into a repeated and collective pattern of hostile online interactions.

heading.text: Key Takeaways

i1.text: Online abuse takes different forms. Offensive speech, hate speech, and digital hostility help us recognise different ways harmful behaviour can appear and develop online.

i2.text: Context matters. Consider the language being used, who or what is being targeted, and the pattern of interactions when identifying online abuse.

i3.text: Different forms of abuse can overlap. A single interaction may involve more than one behaviour, and its characteristics can change as the situation develops.

i4.text: Online abuse can escalate. A single harmful post can develop into repeated or collective hostility as others comment, share, repost, or amplify the content.

i5.text: Some people face disproportionate risk. Identity, visibility, role, and other contextual factors can affect who is targeted and the nature or intensity of the abuse they experience.

i6.text: Recognition is the first step towards action. Understanding what online abuse looks like helps people identify harmful situations and respond more effectively.

body.text: High public visibility can make athletes frequent targets of online abuse. Hateful reactions may arise from sporting outcomes, public perceptions, or interpretations of an athlete’s performance, actions, or personal decisions. These reactions can escalate quickly, allowing harmful content to spread across digital platforms.

Officials can face online abuse following decisions made during competition, adding to the verbal and physical abuse they may already experience in person. Repeated criticism, threats, and hostility can contribute to stress and affect their confidence, perceived authority, and wellbeing.

Journalists play an important role in connecting athletes, teams, and sporting organisations with wider audiences. Journalists may become targets of online hostility in response to their reporting, commentary or perceived position on an issue.

Sporting organisations and the people who fund, manage, and represent them can also become targets of online abuse. Hostile content may be directed at an organisation itself, its decisions, policies or actions, or at individual staff and representatives. This can affect organisational reputation, professional activity, decision-making, and the wellbeing of those involved.

The effects of online abuse can extend to the families and loved ones of those targeted. They may witness the abuse and its impact, become indirect targets through their association with the person experiencing abuse, or receive harmful messages directed at them personally. These experiences can also increase concern and fear for the safety and wellbeing of someone close to them.

Fans are the largest group in sport and are often overlooked. They can be affected by the abuse they encounter within sporting communities, even when they are not a direct target. Identity-based abuse aimed at an athlete, official, or other public figure can also affect fans who share that identity, contributing to an environment in which they may feel unwelcome or unsafe.

body.text: Receiving online abuse can trigger feelings of fear, sadness, anger, and frustration. For athletes, these experiences may also raise concerns about their reputation, career opportunities, relationships with family and friends, and team performance. When abuse occurs publicly, its visibility and potential spread can further intensify psychological distress.

heading.text: Key Takeaways

i1.text: Online abuse can have wide-ranging effects. Its impact can extend across wellbeing, confidence, sense of safety, performance, participation, and other areas of a person’s life.

i2.text: The effects can be interconnected. Emotional distress, disrupted sleep, reduced confidence, safety concerns, and difficulties with focus can overlap and influence one another.

i3.text: People can be affected differently. Personal and contextual factors can shape how someone experiences and responds to online abuse.

i4.text: The impact extends beyond those directly targeted. Families, teammates, colleagues, fans, organisations, and others across sporting communities can also experience its consequences.

i5.text: Online abuse can affect participation and sporting culture. Persistent hostility can influence who feels safe, welcome, and able to participate in sport.

i6.text: The consequences can extend beyond sport. When discriminatory and abusive behaviours become normalised, they can reinforce prejudice, exclusion, and hostility in wider society.

section1Body.text:
Understanding how online abuse affects people helps us build empathy for those targeted and respond with care and respect. The effects of online abuse on people can be serious and far-reaching: a single post can leave someone feeling anxious, unsafe, or doubting themselves even long after the initial interaction.

As abuse continues or spreads across digital platforms, its impact can intensify. Online abuse can affect mental health and wellbeing, as well as how athletes perform, how officials approach decisions, and how journalists and other professionals engage with their work.

Such effects can also extend beyond the person being targeted. Families, teammates, colleagues, and fans may witness or experience the consequences of abuse. At a wider level, persistent online hostility can shape sporting culture, affect participation, and influence who feels safe and welcome in sport.
section1Body.note: Section body on Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact

section2Body.text: High-profile athletes tend to face a large volume of online abuse. However, athletes are not the only people targeted.
section2Body.note: Section body on Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact

section3Body.text: Online abuse can affect everyone involved in sport. Its consequences vary depending on the individual and their circumstances, with some impacts being particularly relevant to athletes. These effects can also reinforce one another: anxiety may disrupt sleep, poor sleep may affect concentration and confidence, and these combined effects can influence daily activities, sporting performance, and overall wellbeing.
section3Body.note: Section body on Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact

section5Body.text:
The effects of online abuse can extend beyond individuals, shaping the culture of sport and the communities around it. Widespread hostility can affect who feels welcome, safe, and able to participate, with implications for inclusion and the sustainability of sporting communities.

Sport also has a wider social influence. The behaviours and attitudes expressed in sporting spaces can contribute to broader social norms. When discriminatory or abusive behaviour becomes normalised, it can reinforce prejudice, exclusion, and hostility beyond sport.
section5Body.note: Section body on Online Abuse in Sport: The Human Impact

i1.text: Assess the situation and your safety. Consider the nature of the content and whether you or someone else may be at immediate risk. If there is an immediate threat, seek appropriate assistance without delay.

i2.text: Collect evidence. Save copies of abusive posts, messages, profile information, URLs, and screenshots before the content is deleted or becomes inaccessible. Keep these records in a secure location in case they are needed for reporting or further action.

i3.text: Record key details. Record when and where the abuse occurred, the accounts involved, and any relevant circumstances. Note whether similar incidents have happened before or whether the behaviour appears to be part of a pattern of abuse.

i4.text: Use platform safety tools. Restrict, mute, or block accounts to limit further contact or exposure to harmful content. Adjust your privacy settings where appropriate to help prevent repeated incidents.

i5.text: Report through the platform. Review the platform’s policies and use its reporting tools to flag abusive content or accounts. Provide relevant details and supporting evidence where requested to help the platform assess the report.

i6.text: Seek additional support or escalate when needed. Contact your organisation’s welfare or safeguarding lead or other appropriate support services. If your safety is threatened, contact local authorities or emergency services as appropriate, regardless of whether you have completed the other steps.

heading.text: Key Takeaways

i1.text: Platform design influences how content spreads. Different digital environments shape who encounters content, how people interact with it, and how long it remains visible.

i2.text: Online harm can be amplified. Recommendation systems, sharing, live interaction, and community dynamics can increase the reach and intensity of harmful content.

i3.text: Abusive tactics can adapt. Harmful content may use altered language, visual formats, indirect targeting, or different digital spaces to make detection more difficult.

i4.text: People can take steps to reduce exposure. Privacy controls, interaction settings, blocking, muting, and thoughtful choices about online spaces can support digital wellbeing.

i5.text: Effective reporting follows a clear process. Assess the situation, document relevant evidence, report through an appropriate channel, and seek support or escalate when safety is at risk.

i6.text: AI has a dual role. It can increase the scale and sophistication of harmful content, and it can also support detection, moderation, and other online safety measures.

i7.text: Technology alone cannot address online abuse. Effective responses combine platform tools, responsible user behaviour, human judgement, organisational support, and appropriate regulation.

What it can cover: Disputes involving legal rights between individuals or organisations, which may include defamation, harassment, misuse of private information, or other privacy-related claims.

html.text: Online abuse can cross national borders immediately. The person targeted, the person responsible, and the platform may all be located in different jurisdictions, with different laws and enforcement processes.

Accounts may use pseudonyms, false identities, or limited identifying information, making it difficult to determine who is responsible for particular behaviour. Identifying an account holder can require information held by platforms and, in some cases, formal legal processes.

The volume and speed of online activity can make investigation and enforcement difficult. Available resources, specialist expertise, evidentiary requirements, and enforcement priorities can all affect what happens after an incident is reported.

Not all harmful or abusive behaviour constitutes a legal offence or provides grounds for legal action. The applicable legal definitions, evidence, context, and jurisdiction all matter.

Legal action is therefore only one part of the response to online abuse. Online platform policies and sporting organisations’ own standards and procedures can also help address behaviours that may not meet the legal requirements for action.

html.text:
In the UK, several laws address harmful online conduct. The Online Safety Act 2023 establishes duties for regulated platforms to address illegal content and protect children from harmful material. It also introduces offences relating to threatening communications, cyberflashing, and sharing or threatening to share intimate images without consent.

The Protection from Harassment Act 1997 addresses harassment and stalking, including behaviour involving digital communications.

The applicable legal protections depend on the nature of the conduct and the relevant jurisdiction.

Source: Legislation.gov.uk

In the United States, online abuse is addressed through a combination of federal and state laws. Federal legislation, including 18 U.S.C. 2261A, addresses certain forms of cyberstalking involving electronic communications. Other federal provisions cover threats and specific forms of online harassment, while state laws may provide additional protections against cyberbullying, harassment, stalking, and non-consensual sharing of intimate images. Legal definitions, enforcement, and available remedies vary by jurisdiction and the circumstances of each case.

Source: U.S. Code

Czech law does not rely on a single offence of “online abuse”. Existing legislation can apply to specific harmful behaviours carried out online. For example, Section 354 of the Czech Criminal Code (Act No. 40/2009 Coll.) addresses stalking, including conduct carried out through electronic communications. Czech Police guidance on stalking explains this provision and identifies repeated social media messages, threats, misuse of personal data, and reputational attacks among behaviours that may occur in stalking cases.

The Czech Civil Code (Act No. 89/2012 Coll.) also protects personality rights, including a person’s dignity, honour and privacy. A person affected by unlawful interference can seek to have the interference stopped and its consequences remedied.

Source: e-Sbírka

Spain’s Criminal Code (Organic Law 10/1995) addresses several forms of online abuse. Article 172 ter covers stalking, including repeated unwanted contact, misuse of personal data and the creation of fake social-media profiles using someone’s image without consent when this causes harassment or humiliation.

Article 510 addresses online hate speech, with increased penalties for certain offences when digital platforms make the content accessible to a large audience.

Victims can report suspected offences to the Spanish National Police or Civil Guard (Guardia Civil). Additional support is available through INCIBE’s free, confidential 017 helpline, while the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) provides a Priority Channel for requesting the urgent removal of unlawfully shared sexual or violent content.

Source: Gobierno de España

In Sweden, online hate or abuse is not a separate legal category. The Swedish Police explains that the same criminal laws generally apply to conduct online as they do offline, with relevant offences potentially including unlawful threats, harassment, defamation, insult, unlawful invasion of privacy, sexual harassment, unlawful identity misuse (e.g. fake profiles in someone else's name), and agitation against a population group. If an offence is motivated by, for example, the victim's ethnicity, religion or sexual orientation, this is an aggravating circumstance in sentencing.

Swedish law also recognises unlawful persecution, which can arise from repeated criminal acts against the same person. Police guidance specifically advises people experiencing stalking to preserve emails, text messages, call records and other digital communications as potential evidence.

Sources: polisen.se; Swedish Parliament

Slovenian law addresses online abuse through existing legislation covering specific harmful behaviours. A particularly relevant example is Article 134a of the Slovenian Criminal Code (KZ-1), which defines stalking to include repeated attempts to establish unwanted contact through electronic communications, where the conduct causes fear or a sense of threat. Slovenian authorities have also recognised the online dimension of stalking in guidance concerning the application of this provision.

Slovenian Police guidance recognises online violence as including behaviours such as threats, harassment, spreading false or insulting content, misuse of photographs, impersonation and the creation of harmful fake profiles. Whether particular conduct constitutes a criminal offence depends on the circumstances of the individual case.

Source: GOV.SI

body.text:
For everyone participating in sport and its online communities:

  • Manage your exposure. Review privacy and safety settings and control who can contact, mention, or tag you.
  • Use safety tools. Mute, restrict, block, and report harmful accounts or content.
  • Preserve evidence. Save relevant information when behaviour may need to be reported or escalated.
  • Protect your wellbeing. You can choose to take a break from online interactions and seek support from people you trust.
Why does this matter?

Your wellbeing matters, and support is a shared responsibility. When people use safety and wellbeing tools, they are better equipped to prevent harm within the wider sporting community.

As a teammate, colleague, fan, friend, or bystander:

  • Avoid amplification. Prevent further circulation of abusive content.
  • Check in privately. Offer personal support to the person targeted.
  • Report appropriately. Take action through established channels, generally without public confrontation.
  • Speak up safely. Express concern about abusive behaviour or seek help from someone who can intervene, including organisational authorities or the police when necessary.
Why does this matter?

Supporting others strengthens the sporting community. Small actions from teammates, colleagues, friends, fans, and other bystanders can help create a social support system where people feel heard, protected, and cared for, and harmful behaviour is less likely to go unchallenged.

body.text:
When responding to online abuse, consider the situation, personal safety, and whether additional support is needed:

  • Assess the situation. Consider the nature of the behaviour, whether it is escalating, and whether anyone may be at risk.
  • Avoid unsafe engagement. Do not confront or engage directly, as it can increase harm or place someone at risk.
  • Know when to seek support. Involve a trusted person or the appropriate organisational contact when the situation requires additional help.
  • Escalate safety concerns. Threats, repeated unwanted contact, exposure of personal information, or other safety concerns may require further organisational or external support.
Why does this matter?

Acting safely helps connect individual action with the right level of support. Recognising when a situation requires additional help allows others to become involved and helps ensure that safety remains the priority.

reveal.text:
About 90%
The UAOA Barometer shows that about nine in ten sporting federations surveyed expressed concern that online abuse could drive talented athletes out of sport. Online abuse can ultimately influence whether people continue participating in sporting communities.

prompt.text: According to research, which of the following effects has online harassment been linked to among athletes?

c0.text: Psychological distress

c1.text: Fewer friends

c2.text: More training hours

reveal.text: Greater exposure to online harassment has been associated with higher levels of psychological distress, highlighting how hostile online content can affect psychological wellbeing.

prompt.text: When a harmful comment about an athlete appears online, which features can influence how far it travels?

c0.text: Platform design and recommendation systems

c1.text: User interactions and reporting mechanisms

c2.text: Both

reveal.text: Both. Platform design, recommendation systems, user interactions, and reporting mechanisms can influence how harmful content travels and reaches new audiences.

prompt.text: A player receives humiliating comments after a loss. Similar messages continue to flood their account for days, including attacks based on their race.Which types of online abuse are occurring in this situation?

c0.text: Offensive speech only

c1.text: Digital hostility and hate speech only

c2.text: Several forms of online abuse are overlapping

reveal.text:
Several forms can overlap.
The humiliating language is offensive speech, the repeated public aggression creates digital hostility, and racist targeting may constitute hate speech.

prompt.text: What is the best recommendation for staying safe when someone encounters online abuse?

c0.text: Respond directly to stop the behaviour

c1.text: Assess the situation, avoid unsafe engagement, and report appropriately

c2.text: Delete the content and leave the platform

reveal.text:
Act safely and use the right reporting channels.
Assess whether the behaviour is escalating or anyone may be at risk, avoid unsafe engagement, preserve relevant evidence, and report through the appropriate platform or organisational channels. Seek additional support when needed.

prompt.text: Can existing laws help protect people from online abuse, including abuse involving AI-generated content?

c0.text: Yes, but protections vary between countries.

c1.text: Only when the abuse involves physical threats.

c2.text: Only when the content is shared publicly.

reveal.text:
Laws can help protect people from online abuse.
However, legal protections and responsibilities vary between countries. Some jurisdictions have introduced specific measures addressing AI-generated intimate images and other forms of digital abuse.

next.text: Laws are only part of the response. What else can we do?

prompt.text: A teammate has been receiving abusive messages and seems increasingly distressed.What is the strongest response from a supportive system?

c0.text: Share the messages publicly so others can defend them

c1.text: Check in privately and help them access appropriate support

c2.text: Limit interactions with the teammate

reveal.text:
Support starts with you!
Check in privately, avoid amplifying the abuse, use appropriate reporting channels, and speak up when it is safe to do so.

prompt.text: Positive action starts with each of us. What can we do?

c0.text: Protect yourself, Support others, Act safely

c1.text: Monitor content, Confront abuser, Delete evidence

c2.text: Report everything, Respond publicly, Stay online

reveal.text:
Protect yourself. Support others. Act safely.
We can manage our social media exposure, use safety tools, preserve evidence, support others who are targeted, and recognise when a situation requires additional help.

prompt.text:
Organisations have a role too. Several people in a sporting organisation have reported online abuse.
What would create the strongest organisational response?

c0.text: Focus primarily on responding to individual incidents

c1.text: Build frameworks, strengthen safeguarding and coordinate action

c2.text: Expect the platforms to manage the problem

reveal.text: Effective organisational responses connect preparation, protection, response and cooperation.

prompt.text: Online abuse is also shaped by conditions beyond any one person or organisation.Which can influence whether harmful behaviour is normalised, challenged or prevented?

c0.text: Education and community norms

c1.text: Research and policies

c2.text: Technology and AI solutions

reveal.text:
All of these. Education, shared standards, research and evidence, policy and law, technological solutions and platform design, and community norms can all shape online behaviour.

Sport is influenced by these wider social conditions, and sporting communities can also help shape the world we live in together.

body.text:
Sport connects millions of people across countries, cultures, and generations through passion, pride, and the thrill of competition.

Online abuse puts that connection at risk. When athletes, officials, volunteers, and fans are attacked online for who they are or how they perform, the consequences can extend far beyond the screen - hurting people, derailing careers, and normalising abusive behaviour.

United Against Online Abuse (UAOA), founded by FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem, brings together more than 75 governments, sporting organisations, academic institutions, and technology platforms around a shared goal: making sport safer from online abuse. Lasting change requires action across institutions, communities, and individuals, and that includes you.

Developed in collaboration with the University of Notre Dame, this eLearning Course will help you recognise different forms of online abuse, understand their impact on your sporting community, and use reporting procedures with confidence. By completing the course, you will be better prepared to take informed action and contribute to a safer sporting environment.

Your journey towards a safer sporting environment starts here.
